blocks.text: Four of Wesgro's eight strategy statements bear directly on this study (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p5). The first sets the destination proposition: Cape Town and the Western Cape "top of mind as a leading business and tourism destination with premium products and services". The fourth names new markets and buyers in China, ASEAN, India, Brazil and the Middle East, "while maintaining a continued focus on established markets". The sixth commits Wesgro to "Track and address systemic challenges influencing economic competitiveness", and the seventh to "Provide economic data, insights & analytics for the Western Cape". The strategy's growth-market work, focus area 4, centres on two of them: India and China, whose travellers already reach Cape Town through Gulf and African hubs (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p46, p48). The growth model's acceleration group holds the Gulf, China, India and Brazil (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20).

Three pillars carry the tree: Reshape demand, Transform supply and Build enabling capability. Each pillar holds two themes, and the six themes hold twenty focus areas [Summary of Findings, 14 Oct 2026, pp15 to 16: deck not in hand; page citation to confirm]. blocks.text: The workstreams divide the tree between them. The demand and aviation work tested five of the six demand focus areas and the case for routes and seats. The infrastructure work tested cruise, mobility, product, visitor experience and capital. The inclusion work tested community inclusion and, with the stakeholder and infrastructure work, bookability. The stakeholder engagement supplied most of the evidence on climate risk, the flagship nature sites and the governance theme. The twentieth focus area, workforce and service skills, has no workstream yet. The 300,000-jobs ambition has no labour analysis behind it (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p4). Section 1.1 asks Wesgro and DEDAT to commission one in 2027.

blocks.text: Wesgro runs the demand side of this system through six units: Cape Town Air Access, Cruise Cape Town, the Convention Bureau, Destination Marketing, Research and Tourism (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p7). Around them sit fifteen external organisations across three spheres of government and industry (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p7; organisations as shown on the stakeholder map and grouped by this report).

The levers that bind the system sit with those partners. National government and its agencies, among them South African Tourism, ACSA and Transnet, hold visa rules, air service agreements, route rights and airport and port operations. The province holds jobs, inclusion and spatial outcomes, sector development, safety programmes and infrastructure planning. The City delivers services, manages precincts and readies events. Industry, from Cape Town Tourism, the V&A Waterfront and the flagship sites to the cruise lines and hotels, holds route viability, demand generation and product standards (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58).

Alignment across those tiers is thin. Stakeholders described strain at SA Tourism and a lack of fiscal space (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). More than twenty bodies produce tourism data and "there is no single view of visitor behaviour, making strategy reactive rather than predictive" (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p56, p57). Fifteen of the sixteen organisations interviewed raised industry and government collaboration, and the Department of Economic Development named restrictive bilateral air agreements and below-peer destination funding as high-impact constraints (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46, p24, p25; the count is of organisations with at least one insight under the theme).
